near_miss.lead: ON ausa vatni (ok gefa nafn) ~ Hom. ἀφυσσάμεθ' ὕδωρ, *h2ews- + *wodr- 'draw water'
near_miss.why_not: ON 'ausa vatni' (instr. dat.) is the pre-Christian naming rite, 'sprinkle a child with water', while Homer's ἀφύσσομαι ὕδωρ means fetching water; the contexts don't match. The ἀφύσσω ~ *h2ews- equation is itself doubtful, and 'draw water' is everyday wording. Collocates --pair: the Germanic hits are all naming-rite formulae, the Greek ones Odyssey watering stops. The Irish partners (do thabairt uisce; naming of a spring, ca ferr ainm) have no cognate wording.

near_miss.lead: ON um nóttina ... í svefni sá hann ~ Lat. hac nocte in somnis visus sum videre: *h1en + loc. of *swepno- + 'see', dream-vision
near_miss.why_not: The prepositional phrase is cognate (í svefni ~ in somnis), but 'saw in sleep at night' is universal dream-report language. The verbs are not cognate (siá vs videre). Collocates of *swep- show night/sleep association in every branch but no distinctive 'see' partner. The ON text is a hagiographic dream vision with Latin models, and Il. 9.325 / Od. 19.340 ἀΰπνους νύκτας is a different figure.
Only the verb is cognate; the objects differ (orð vs λόγοι), and 'hear the words' is generic.

near_miss.lead: ekki vápn festi á honom ~ ἐν χροῒ πήγνυτο 'weapons stuck in the body'
near_miss.why_not: ON festa < *fastaz is not securely from *peh2ǵ- (πήγνυμι). The ON text is negated invulnerability magic (fjǫlkunnigr); Homer has spears fixed in flesh. Generic battle description.
Only *werǵom is cognate; stórr is not cognate with μέγας. Prose 'great task' is generic; no congruent context.

near_miss.lead: Kin lists: father~son, mother~daughter (do-ceiled athair ar a mac ⁊ máthair ar ingin ~ ни оч҃ь сн҃ови ни мт҃и дъчери); athair ⁊ máthair ⁊ derbráthair ~ pitā bhrātā mātā
near_miss.why_not: The kin terms are cognate but kin lists are a generic merism. The contexts differ: in the Irish, secrecy while building Dind Ríg; in the Russian, famine breakdown, probably biblical (Mt 10:21, Micah 7:6) rather than inherited. Genealogical ON passages are formulaic only within ON.

near_miss.lead: welcome 'for the sake of father and mother' (fáilti ... daig t'athar ⁊ do mathar)
near_miss.why_not: No cognate partner outside Irish; the ON passage is genealogy plus 'góðr fagnaðr', not cognate.

near_miss.lead: kingly name refused; poet praising; skaldic 'blóð kom varmt' / 'vǫll ... vá'
near_miss.why_not: Read closely: partners share only frequent roots (or mis-mapped ones: fili/vǫllr/lorum on *wel-, gal/vega on *weyk-). No shared wording.

'ól Bergliót ... sveinbarn' = Bergljót bore a boy
'siá í svefni man einn' = saw a man in his sleep
